title: They were arguing… while Jesus was bleeding in His heart for them.
paragraphs: They were arguing… while Jesus was bleeding in His heart for them.
Let that sit.

Not pagans.
Not strangers.
Disciples.

Men who saw the blind see.
Men who heard the Sermon on the Mount with their own ears.
Men who held bread that multiplied in their hands.
And still—
They wanted the spotlight.
“A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest.” — Luke 22:24
This is not just a story.
This is a mirror.
Because if we’re honest… this spirit still lives today.

In churches.
In ministries.
Even in quiet hearts that never say it out loud.
We don’t always shout, “I want to be the greatest.”
But we feel it.

When someone else gets recognized… and something in us tightens.
When another person is used by God… and we compare instead of celebrate.
When we serve faithfully… but secretly hope someone notices.
That’s not hunger for God.
That’s hunger for position.
And here’s the tension that should shake us:

While they were debating greatness…
Jesus was preparing for the cross.

While they were measuring status…
He was about to be stripped of everything.

While they were climbing…
He was descending into suffering.
Feel the weight of that contrast.
Because this is where pride becomes dangerous.
It blinds you to what Jesus is actually doing.
You can be near Him… and still miss Him.
You can hear His words… and still chase your own glory.
You can be chosen… and still be competing.
That’s the warning.
But don’t miss the turn.
Jesus doesn’t cancel them.
He corrects them—with grace that cuts deep.
“Let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves.” — Luke 22:26
In other words:
You want greatness?
Then go lower.
You want influence?
Then pick up the towel.
You want to lead?
Then become the servant no one applauds.
And then He drops the truth that shatters every ego:
“I am among you as the one who serves.” — Luke 22:27
This is not just instruction.
This is revelation.

The King of Heaven—serving.
The Creator—kneeling.
The Holy One—washing dirty feet.

Feet that would run away.
Feet that would deny Him.
Feet that would scatter when He needed them most.
Still—He served.
That is not weakness.
That is divine strength wrapped in humility.
And this is where the Gospel explodes with beauty:
Jesus didn’t just model humility.
He paid for our pride.
Because the truth is—we are not just like the disciples.
We are worse.

We don’t just struggle with pride.
We build identities around it.
We protect it.
We justify it.
We disguise it as “confidence,” “calling,” or even “ministry.”
But pride cannot stand before a holy God.
It must be crucified.
And that’s exactly where Jesus was going.
To the cross.

Not just to forgive obvious sins—
but to break the invisible ones.

Comparison.
Jealousy.
Self-exaltation.
The need to be seen.
He carried it all.

And when He said, “It is finished,”
He made a way for proud hearts to become clean hearts.
For restless, competing souls to finally rest.

For people obsessed with greatness…
to be transformed into people who reflect His greatness.
So here’s the question:
Where are you in this story?

Are you quietly competing?
Are you serving—but checking who’s watching?
Are you struggling to rejoice when others rise?
Don’t ignore that.
That’s not just personality.
That’s a place where Jesus wants to meet you.
Not with shame.
But with invitation.
Come down.
Come lower.
Come closer to the cross.
Because in the Kingdom of God, the way up… is always down.

And the ones who kneel with Jesus
will rise with Him in ways the world can never replicate.
This is not about losing your worth.
It’s about finding it in the right place.

Not in titles.
Not in applause.
Not in being “the greatest.”
But in being His.

Fully forgiven.
Fully seen.
Fully loved.
So today—

Lay down the comparison.
Release the need to be recognized.
Repent where pride has taken root.
And pick up the towel.
Because real greatness is not proven on a stage.
It’s revealed in surrender.

And Jesus is still looking for hearts
that would rather be faithful… than famous.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
